readerTitle: Amazon's quiet profit engine: why a dollar of sales isn't a dollar
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon 2023 연간 실적: AWS와 나머지 사업) + 가상 적용 (포장 상자 제조사)
insight: 매출의 크기는 사업의 중요도를 말해 주지 않는다. 매출 1달러에서 얼마가 남는지(마진)를 봐야 어디서 돈을 버는지 보인다.
misconception: 매출이 큰 사업이 돈도 더 많이 번다. 그리고 마진은 높을수록 무조건 좋다.

sources.text: Amazon.com, Inc. Form 10-K for fiscal year 2023 (segment information: North America, International, AWS)
포장 상자 제조사 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Amazon 2023 10-K 수치 재확인 필요: 총매출 $574.8B, 총영업이익 $36.9B, AWS 매출 $90.8B, AWS 영업이익 $24.6B. 나머지(북미+해외) 매출 574.8 − 90.8 = $484.0B, 영업이익 36.9 − 24.6 = $12.2B(북미 약 $14.9B, 해외 약 −$2.7B).
'나머지' 부문에는 온라인·오프라인 매장뿐 아니라 광고, 구독(Prime), 판매자 서비스가 포함됩니다. 광고는 마진이 높은 것으로 알려져 있으나 Amazon이 부문별 이익을 따로 공개하지 않으므로 카드에는 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Amazon's quiet profit engine
body: In 2023, Amazon brought in about $575 billion in sales. Most of that came from selling and shipping goods.
Yet about two-thirds of its operating profit came from a part of the company most shoppers never see: renting out computing power to other businesses.

image.label: A huge warehouse next to a small, glowing server room
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 상자가 가득한 거대한 물류창고, 오른쪽에 작은 서버실. 서버실 쪽에서 금화가 더 많이 흘러나오는 장면. 실제 기업 로고, 화살표 미소 마크, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which part made more profit?
body: Amazon reports its business in parts. In 2023:
**The store side** (selling, shipping, ads, subscriptions) had about $484 billion in sales. **AWS**, its cloud computing arm, had about $91 billion.
Which part made more operating profit, the money left after running the business?

options.text: The store side. It sold more than five times as much
options.feedback: Size feels like the safe bet. But sales only tell you how much money came in, not how much of it stayed.
Right. AWS made about $24.6 billion. The much bigger store side made about $12.2 billion.

options.text: Roughly the same, since big sales balance out lower prices
options.feedback: Good instinct that the gap in sales doesn't mean a gap in profit. But the smaller part earned about twice as much.

cards.title: Small in sales, big in profit.
body: AWS was about one in six dollars of Amazon's sales, and about two in three dollars of its operating profit.

image.label: AWS is small in sales, large in profit
image.brief: Sales stores $484B vs AWS $91B; profit stores $12B vs AWS $25B.

cards.title: Margin
body: **Margin** is the share of each sales dollar you keep after costs, shown as a percentage.
On the store side, each dollar of sales left about 2.5 cents of operating profit. At AWS, each dollar left about 27 cents. Same dollar coming in, ten times more staying.
You'll often see two versions. **Gross margin** counts only the cost of what you sold. **Operating margin** also subtracts the cost of running the business, like staff and offices.

image.label: Two dollar bills: a thin slice kept vs a thick slice kept
image.brief: 지폐 두 장을 나란히. 왼쪽 지폐는 아주 얇은 조각만 초록색으로 표시 "2.5¢ kept", 오른쪽 지폐는 4분의 1 이상이 초록색 "27¢ kept". 나머지 부분은 회색으로 "Costs" 라벨.

cards.title: Margin depends on what each sale drags along.
body: Ask what has to happen every time you make one more sale.
list: **Selling goods:** buy the item, store it, pack it, ship it. Costs grow almost as fast as sales.
**Renting computing power:** data centers are expensive to build, but once built, many more customers can share them. Each new dollar of sales needs much less new cost.
**Price power:** customers who depend on a service and find switching hard leave more room to charge.
cards.callout: Two businesses can grow sales at the same speed and keep very different amounts.

cards.title: A thin margin isn't always a problem.
body: A low margin can be a deliberate choice. Low prices can bring huge volume and loyal customers, and many retailers and distributors run on thin margins on purpose. A thin margin on very large sales can still pay the bills.
Percent and dollars tell different stories. Forty percent of a tiny business pays fewer bills than five percent of a huge one.
And a very high margin draws rivals, who may try to win your customers by cutting price.

cards.title: Now it's a box factory.
body: You make cardboard boxes. Plain stock boxes bring in $2 million a year at an 8% gross margin: $160,000. Custom printed boxes bring in $600,000 at a 35% margin: $210,000.
You're setting next year's goal for the sales team. Which goal do you pick?

options.text: Grow total sales 20%, whatever the product
options.feedback: Easy to track, but most of that growth will likely come from stock boxes, the easiest sale. You could hit the goal and barely grow profit.

options.text: Grow gross profit dollars, and pay sales bonuses on profit, not sales
options.feedback: This steers effort toward custom work without throwing away the stock box business. You still need to check that the factory has room for more printing jobs.

options.text: Drop stock boxes and sell only custom work
options.feedback: The margin percentage would jump. But you'd give up $160,000 a year and the steady orders that keep machines busy.

cards.title: Ask what each dollar keeps, not just how many dollars come in.
body: Sales show how big a business is. Margin shows where the money is actually made.
**Try it today:** list your two or three main products or services. For each, estimate sales and what's left after the costs of delivering it. Is your biggest seller also your biggest earner?
